standard.title: Roles and groups in ancient society
standard.description: the organisation and roles of key groups in ancient society such as the nobility, bureaucracy, women and slaves, and how they influenced and changed society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explain how the physical environment shaped the development of the ancient society, including agricultural foundations and social complexity (AC9HH7K09). They have not yet examined the internal social organisation of the ancient society — the specific groups, their roles, their relationships, and how power was distributed and contested.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students describe the organisation and roles of key social groups in the ancient society — including the nobility, bureaucracy, women, and slaves — explain how these groups influenced the society, and describe how the relationships between groups changed over time.

nodes.label: Social hierarchy and the nobility and bureaucracy
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the social hierarchy of the ancient society, the roles of the nobility and bureaucracy, and explain how these groups exercised power and shaped the society's organisation.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the roles of the nobility and bureaucracy in the ancient society and explain how they exercised power.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the social hierarchy of the ancient society — how it was structured, who sat at its apex (ruler, pharaoh, emperor, council), and how the nobility and bureaucracy exercised power through land, taxation, military command, and administration. Explain how these groups maintained their position and how their roles shaped the daily organisation of society.
wider: Examine the mechanisms of power in the ancient society in detail — how the nobility justified their position (divine right, military prowess, heredity), what the bureaucracy actually did (tax collection, record-keeping, law enforcement), and how these mechanisms were similar to or different from power structures in other ancient societies.

Investigate how the social hierarchy was made visible — in art, architecture, burial practices, clothing, and ceremony — and what these representations tell us about how the society understood its own structure.
Explore cases where bureaucratic or noble power was contested or changed — internal conflicts, reform attempts, dynastic changes — as evidence that social hierarchies were not fixed.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students without a concrete knowledge base of noble and bureaucratic roles and their mechanisms of power cannot analyse women's constrained influence (N2) or slaves' structural contribution (N3) — the social architecture must be established before the groups within it can be meaningfully positioned.

response_modes.reason: Students need a concrete knowledge base of specific social groups and their roles before they can reason about influence, change, and contested power. Without knowing what the nobility and bureaucracy actually did — their specific functions, their relationship to each other and to lower groups — later nodes about women, slaves, and social change lack an anchor.

success_criteria: Describes the roles of both the nobility and bureaucracy with reference to specific functions (land, taxation, military, administration).
Explains how these groups exercised and maintained power — not just that they had power, but how.
Correctly describes the social hierarchy — understands it as layered, with different groups occupying different positions.

nodes.label: Women's roles and their influence
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the roles of women in the ancient society, identify sources of evidence about women's lives, and explain how women influenced the society despite structural constraints.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the typical roles of women in the ancient society and identify at least one way in which women exercised influence.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the structural position of women in the ancient society — their typical roles in household, religious, and economic life — and explain how women exercised influence within and sometimes beyond these roles. Note that evidence about women's lives is often limited and how this affects historical interpretation.
wider: Examine specific women who exercised significant power or influence in the ancient society — such as Hatshepsut, Cleopatra, or figures from Mesopotamian, Greek, Roman, or Chinese contexts — analysing how they navigated, expanded, or challenged their structural constraints.

Investigate the sources of evidence available about women's lives in the ancient society — what types of sources exist, what groups of women are documented, and what is missing — and examine what the gaps in evidence reveal about whose stories were preserved.

Compare the structural position and actual influence of women across two or three ancient societies, identifying patterns and differences that complicate any simple characterisation of 'women in the ancient world'.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly apply a single, undifferentiated characterisation of women in ancient societies — either 'had no power' or use exceptional figures like Cleopatra to claim full agency. Multiple examples — different societies, different social classes, different types of evidence — resolve this binary. Breadth across social groups (elite women, women in commerce, women in religious roles) and evidence types builds a more accurate, differentiated picture.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The analysis of women's roles in ancient societies is inherently rich — it raises questions about evidence, perspective, and the limits of what we can know. Advancing students can engage with the methodological challenge of writing history about groups who are systematically underrepresented in the surviving record, and with the insight that limited evidence does not mean limited importance or agency. This also connects directly to the S06 descriptor (perspectives in sources).
success_criteria: Describes at least two aspects of women's roles in the ancient society.
Identifies that evidence about women's lives is often limited, and explains how this affects what historians can claim.
Provides at least one specific example of women's influence — not just that women 'had some influence' in the abstract.

nodes.label: Slaves and other groups — power structures and social influence
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the role of slaves and other marginalised groups in the ancient society, explain how these groups contributed to and influenced the society, and describe how the relationships between social groups changed over time.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the role of slaves in the ancient society and explain how the slave system contributed to the society's functioning.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the role of slaves and the structural conditions of slavery in the ancient society — how people became enslaved, what work they performed, how they were treated, and how the slave system underpinned the economy and social structure. Describe how other non-elite groups (artisans, merchants, farmers) also contributed to and influenced the society. Explain how the composition and relationships of these groups changed over time.
wider: Examine the evidence for how slaves experienced, responded to, and sometimes resisted their condition — including examples of revolt, self-purchase, manumission, and legal status changes — challenging a purely passive account of enslaved people.

Investigate how the slave system shaped other aspects of the society — architecture, cultural production, military capacity, economic specialisation — examining the ways in which slaves' contributions were foundational rather than peripheral.
Explore how the composition and size of enslaved populations changed over time in the ancient society — through conquest, trade, debt — and how changes in these numbers affected social stability.

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the social hierarchy (Node 1) and women's roles (Node 2) into a complete account of the social structure of the ancient society — including how power relationships between all groups influenced and changed the society. Students must coordinate multiple social groups and their interactions into a coherent picture of how the society was organised and how it changed, reaching the descriptor's full demand.

success_criteria: Describes the role of slaves in the ancient society with reference to specific types of work or contributions.
Explains that the social structure involved interdependent groups — not just powerful groups on top of passive groups below.
Describes at least one way in which the relationships between social groups changed over time.
